metric.why: Transformer and switchgear lead times stretched from months to years and now gate construction schedules as hard as permits do. Lead-time surveys are published by industry groups and research firms; watch the directory sources.
metric.definition: Order-to-delivery time for transformers, switchgear, generators, cooling plant, and high-end accelerators.

reading.body:
Critical equipment lead times, not permits, now set the pace of data center construction, with transformers and switchgear stretching from months to years.

The constraint has moved into the supply chain. A data center is a building full of power equipment before it is a building full of servers, and the order-to-delivery time for transformers, switchgear, generators, cooling plant, and high-end accelerators now gates schedules as hard as any approval. When those lead times run to years, capital committed to a project sits idle waiting on hardware rather than on concrete.

For AI specifically, this reframes scaling as a procurement problem alongside a power problem. Compute capacity cannot be installed faster than the electrical gear that feeds and cools it arrives, so accelerator deployments inherit the delivery schedules of transformer and switchgear makers. The binding constraint is not only how much power a site can secure but how long the equipment to use that power takes to show up.

The data here is a definition and a direction, not a measurement. It names the equipment categories and states that lead times stretched from months to years, but gives no figures, no dates, and no breakdown by equipment type or region. It also does not say whether the stretch is easing or worsening. Readers should treat the direction as established and the magnitude as unquantified in this data.
